newsitem.title: UK: British farmer infected by horse manure.
newsitem.headline: British farmer infected by horse manure.

text.p: A British farmer caught a potentially deadly E coli infection from horses he was caring for, researchers said on Friday.
A toxic strain of the E coli bacteria has caused several outbreaks of food poisoning in Britain, most recently killing 20 elderly people in Scotland.
But Dr Rachel Chalmers and colleagues at the Public Health Laboratory Service in Cardiff said the 84-year-old farmer became infected after cleaning horse stalls.

The farmer became sick with bloody diarrhoea, and tests found he was infected with E coli. At first the horse manure was not found to be infected, although it carried salmonella, another source of poisoning.
But two weeks later the horses were found to be carrying E coli.

"Given the high degree of handling and the large numbers of people, particularly children, who have contact with them there is a need for awareness that horses can be a vehicle of (E coli) infection in human beings," they wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
E coli is normally a benign gut bacteria found in a wide range of animals. But one strain, E coli 0157, has become toxic to humans.
Spread mostly through cow faeces contaminating meat or vegetable products, it can cause bloody diarrhoea, kidney failure and death in the vulnerable such as the very old or very young.
Experts said last week it could be destroyed using standard hygiene practices such as hand-washing and the proper use of bleach or other disinfectants.
